title: Compact quantization memory vs latency sweep (Mar 2026)
content:
Purpose:
Run a focused sweep to quantify memory savings vs end-to-end latency/throughput and quality impact for compact (low-bit) quant formats and kernel variants. Goal is to recommend default profiles for Dedicated and Hosted tiers where memory headroom is the constraint (eg. denser models, multi-tenant pools).

Context / motivation:
- Lots of previous work focused on absolute throughput (tokens/sec) for int8 and awq kernels; fewer notes about the operational tradeoff when GPU memory is the binding resource (more models per node, larger context windows).
- We need profiles that answer: if we move from FP16 to INT8/FP8/AWQ/GPTQ, how many concurrent connections/pinned models do we gain, and what is the expected latency penalty at low and high batch pressure?
- This doc is intentionally concise — experimental log + high-level takeaways and next actions. More raw traces are linked in the PR.

Experimental setup (applies to all runs unless noted):
- Hardware: A100 80GB (PCIe fabric) and H100 80GB (NVLink) nodes. 1 GPU per instance.
- OS / drivers: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS 12.x, NCCL 2.18.
- Runtime: serving-runtime dev branch compact-quant-sweep (PR 472).
- Models: Llama2-13B-chat (v1.0), RedCrew-7B (internal distilled), and a single 33B checkpoint used as proxy for >32B behavior.
- Quant formats tested: FP16 baseline, FP8 (E4M3-like path), INT8 (per-channel symmetric and per-tensor dynamic), GPTQ (8->4 and 8->3 variants via offline GPTQ), AWQ (AWQ 4-bit and 3-bit modes).
- Kernel variants: fused matmul (runtime-fused), blocked GEMM pack (pack-k), cuBLAS fallback, and a CUDA-optimized awq-kernel from the awq branch.
- Workload profiles: short chat (prompt 32 tokens, response 64), medium (prompt 128, response 256), and long (prompt 512, response 1024). Also KV-cache warm vs cold experiments.
- Concurrency: single-stream, 4-concurrent streams, and batch sizes 1..8 (dynamic batching enabled).
- Quality metrics: perplexity on WikiText-103 (calibration-only), token-level edit distance vs FP16 baseline on 200 prompt eval set, and small subset of instruction-heavy evals for hallucination signals.
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 latency for first-token and full-response, tokens/sec, GPU memory (used via nvidia-smi sampling), CPU mem, and observed cache miss ratios.

Key results (summary bullets):
- Memory savings: INT8 per-channel and AWQ-4 reduce peak model memory by ~1.9-2.1x vs FP16; AWQ-3/GPTQ-3 get us to ~2.8-3.2x depending on packing. FP8 reductions are ~1.6x but with smaller quant/dequant overhead.
- Latency impact: On A100, INT8 (per-channel) adds ~6-12% median latency and ~10-25% p95 for short and medium response profiles due to dequant and extra kernel launches; on H100 the penalty is smaller (3-8%) for fused kernels.
- AWQ kernels: AWQ-4 with the awq-kernel shows best memory density with modest latency (median +8-15%), but AWQ-3 increases p99 variability significantly under burst concurrency (p99 up to +60% in some traces).
- GPTQ offline quant: highest memory savings for large models but showed the largest quality degradation on instruction-heavy evals (increase in token edit distance ~12-18% vs FP16), and occasional generation artifacts in long-context runs.
- FP8: best latency profile (near parity with FP16) on fused matmul kernels — lower memory savings than INT8/AWQ but attractive when latency is primary constraint.
- KV cache interaction: quant formats that require per-request dequant reduce the benefit of warm KV cache since CPU/GPU transfer overhead dominates for small response sizes. Pack-k kernels that keep dequant inside GPU and reuse cached keys mitigated this.

Representative numbers (Llama2-13B-chat, medium profile, A100):
- FP16 baseline: peak GPU mem 24.8GB, median latency 210ms, p95 480ms, tokens/sec 180
- INT8-per-channel: peak mem 13.1GB, median 230ms, p95 540ms, tokens/sec 160
- AWQ-4 (awq-kernel): peak mem 11.9GB, median 255ms, p95 650ms, tokens/sec 150
- FP8 fused: peak mem 15.2GB, median 220ms, p95 500ms, tokens/sec 175
- GPTQ-3 (offline): peak mem 9.0GB, median 290ms, p95 980ms, tokens/sec 120

Operational observations / failure modes:
- Fragmentation: packing strategies that reduce memory often increase allocator fragmentation for long-lived models in Dedicated pools; this caused OOMs during transient spikes. We need defragmentation hooks in the allocator or a compact-reload path.
- Host staging: quant formats that require additional CPU staging memory (for scales/zeros) pushed node host memory above safe thresholds on multi-model nodes.
- Kernel maturity: cuBLAS fallback path is generally more stable but slower; awq-kernel had a few device-side asserts with sequence lengths >2000 — mitigated by limiting max_ctx in serving config.
- Re-quant at runtime: mixed-precision fallback (selectively upcast hot layers) reduced tail latency but complicated caching and increases calibration overhead.

Quality notes (short):
- GPTQ-3 and AWQ-3 had measurable drop on our instruction eval set; AWQ-4 and INT8 maintained acceptable quality for casual chat prompts.
- Long-context samples showed higher token divergence for ultra-low-bit configs; recommend not using 3-bit variants for >1024 context unless eval coverage exists.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Default hosted profile: FP8-fused for latency-sensitive routes (medium models), AWQ-4 as an opt-in memory-saver profile for multi-tenant pools where slightly higher p95 is tolerable.
2) Dedicated reserved capacity: allow GPTQ-3 for very large (>30B) pinned models where memory is the gating factor, but require per-customer eval + SLA opt-in.
3) Add a "quantization-memory" knob in rollout UI that shows estimated concurrent sessions gained vs expected p95 impact.
4) Prioritize kernel work: implement in-GPU dequant for INT8 path (pack-k style) to reduce host staging and reduce latency penalty.
5) Allocate SRE experiment: run live A/B on 2 Dedicated clusters for 2 weeks to measure real-world p99 and error rates before broad enablement.

Open questions / next steps (short TODOs):
- TODO: run same sweep on H100 with TensorRT fused schedules (Evan Li to lead) — measure p95/p99 delta vs our CUDA kernels.
- TODO: test per-layer mixed-precision schedule automated by optimizer (Marco) and collect quality regressions per-layer.
- TODO: document memory fragmentation mitigation options and estimate rebuild window for Dedicated pools (Priya).
- TODO: expand eval to instruction-heavy suite (2000 examples) to better capture hallucination risk for GPTQ/AWQ-3.

Appendix: quick notes from traces and links
- raw traces and allocation timelines attached in PR 472 (see linked_artifacts).
- sample replay cmd used: ./perf/replay_client --trace traces/short_chat.json --profile compact-quant --concurrency 4 --max-batches 500
- brief hypothesis: when dequant is GPU-internal we get both memory and latency wins; when dequant is host-side the memory wins are real but the latency/variance cost often outweighs them for small responses.

Questions for reviewers:
- Acceptable p95 uplift for Hosted "standard" vs memory gain? (Team input required; propose p95 <= +20% for opt-in memory profiles).
- Is GPTQ allowed for Dedicated without mandatory per-customer evals? (security/legal might require more review).

Notes to self: keep this doc short; long-form raw data in PR. Will follow-up with packed-kernel alloc instrumentation and an H100 run card next week.

¨end of note¨
